clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant keratinising disorder caused by variants in keratin genes KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT16, or KRT17
Hallmark is painful focal plantar keratoderma, which is frequently the most disabling symptom
Hypertrophic nail dystrophy with distal thickening and subungual hyperkeratosis affects most or all nails
Oral leukokeratosis (white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa) is common and can mimic candidiasis
Cysts (steatocystoma or pilosebaceous) and follicular keratoses are frequent, particularly with certain keratin subtypes
Natal or neonatal teeth occur with KRT17-related disease
Genotype influences phenotype, so keratin gene testing helps classify and counsel patients
reference.pathophysiology: Pachyonychia congenita arises from dominant-negative variants in genes encoding the keratins K6a, K6b, K16, and K17, which pair to form the intermediate filament cytoskeleton of specialised epithelia such as palmoplantar skin, nail bed, oral mucosa, and pilosebaceous structures. Mutant keratins disrupt filament assembly and weaken the mechanical resilience of these cells, so they cannot withstand normal physical stress. This provokes reactive hyperproliferation and hyperkeratosis in weight-bearing skin and nails and produces the painful plantar keratoderma, nail thickening, and mucosal and follicular manifestations that characterise the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Onychomycosis and other causes of nail dystrophy
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of the pachyonychia congenita keratin genes
Fungal microscopy and culture of nails to exclude onychomycosis
Skin biopsy of keratoderma or oral lesions when the diagnosis is uncertain
Assessment and photography of nails, soles, and oral mucosa to document extent
Family history and examination of relatives given dominant inheritance
redFlags: Severe plantar pain limiting mobility and function
Secondary bacterial or fungal infection of fissured keratoderma
Laryngeal involvement causing hoarseness or airway symptoms in early-onset severe disease
Persistent oral white plaque needing evaluation to exclude other pathology
reference.prognosis: It is a lifelong condition without effect on life expectancy, but the painful plantar keratoderma often causes chronic disability and reduced mobility; management is supportive, focused on mechanical offloading, keratolysis, and pain control.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating nails for presumed onychomycosis without recognising the genetic disorder
Mistaking oral leukokeratosis for candidiasis or premalignant leukoplakia
Underestimating the impact of plantar pain on daily function and mental health
Failing to offer genetic counselling regarding dominant inheritance
management: Focus on the disabling plantar keratoderma with mechanical offloading, protective footwear and orthotics, and regular paring or debridement of hyperkeratotic skin
Apply keratolytics such as urea or salicylic acid, together with emollients, to soften and reduce keratoderma
Provide pain control for plantar pain with topical measures and analgesics, as pain is often the most disabling symptom
Manage thickened nails with regular podiatric trimming, and consider nail avulsion or ablation for troublesome nails
Treat cysts and oral leukokeratosis symptomatically, distinguishing oral plaques from candidiasis
Consider a trial of oral retinoids in selected cases, recognising the response is variable and may worsen plantar pain
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant keratin disorder, with examination of relatives
